In this study, we delve into large PFMs adaptation in the resource-constrained federated learning environment, and propose an innovative framework, which alternates between large model distillation and resource-adaptive pruning, with guaranteed convergence. Our framework, namely ADRAP, confers a dual advantage. First, the alternating pipeline balances retaining intrinsic PFMs capabilities with assimilating new domain knowledge from local private data. Additionally, our novel distilling-while-adaptive-pruning strategy dynamically accommodates heterogeneous client resources, ensuring effective collaborative optimization under arbitrary constraints. Theoretically, we establish upper bounds for parameter updates during both the distillation and pruning-based adaptation stages and further demonstrate that ADRAP maintains an asymptotically optimal convergence rate $O(1/\sqrt{\rho TQ})$. Empirical results reveal that ADRAP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 14.23% (at $a=0.1$) for NLP tasks and 20.55% (under IID) for CV tasks in average accuracy across both domains, demonstrating its effectiveness and adaptability in federated large model adaptation.
10.1109/tcc.2026.3735701: Federated learning keeps raw data on local devices, but wireless deployments still suffer from substantial communication energy consumption, hierarchy-induced delay, and privacy risks caused by heterogeneous channel conditions. This paper studies a nested federated multi-task architecture with one macro edge server, multiple micro edge servers (mESs), and heterogeneous end clients that maintain both a general task model and a lightweight resource allocation optimization (RAO) model. The RAO model uses round-wise channel and device states to determine subcarrier and power allocation, while the task model performs application-level learning under the allocated communication budget. We reformulate the joint subcarrier and power allocation problem as a constrained energy-minimization problem with explicit rate, power, and assignment constraints, and we further clarify the dual-model computation overhead, the latency impact of the two-level hierarchy, and the scope of privacy computing as FL-based data locality rather than a formal privacy guarantee. To better capture time-varying wireless conditions, the adopted channel model combines Okumura-Hata large-scale path loss with round-wise block fading. Simulation results in medium-scale scenarios show that the proposed nested strategy achieves favorable communication-energy performance and run-to-run stability compared with the implemented heuristic and learning-based baselines, while clarifying the operating assumptions and limitations of the framework.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3734103: This paper presents an asynchronous federated learning framework tailored for inertial measurement unit (IMU) systems. Traditional federated learning methods face substantial challenges when applied to the heterogeneous and time-sensitive characteristics of IMU data collected from wearable and mobile devices. The proposed framework introduces an adaptive asynchronous update mechanism that accounts for device-specific constraints while preserving model performance and convergence guarantees. Extensive experiments on publicly available motion-sensing datasets demonstrate that the method achieves faster convergence and higher macro-F1 than synchronous baselines, with reduced communication overhead. The approach proves particularly effective in human activity recognition and motion analysis applications, where IMU data often exhibit variability in sampling rates, signal quality, and availability. Moreover, the framework maintains robust performance under device heterogeneity and constrained communication budgets, sustaining competitive macro-F1 even under aggressive update compression.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3734977: Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs) for remote health monitoring generate delay-sensitive patient data that requires low-latency processing. However, the limited computational resources of WBAN devices make local data processing challenging. Fog computing addresses this resource limitation problem by enabling data processing closer to patients. However, the limited resources of Fog Servers (FSs) require efficient allocation to reduce latency and energy consumption. Moreover, health data analysis requires accurate processing with minimal loss. Therefore, to address these challenges, this paper formulates a cost-minimization problem keeping latency, energy, and loss function in deliberation. To solve the formulated problem, Cost Minimization Algorithm (CMA) has been proposed using Follow The Perturbed Leader (FTPL) supporting Federated Learning (FL)-based Federated Averaging (FedAvg) technique. The FTPL technique is utilized to select efficient FS, and FedAvg performs processing of WBAN data accurately with minimized loss function value. Through experimental and prototype demonstrations, the efficacy of proposed CMA framework is shown by achieving a 40.05% reduction in the average total cost compared to other State-of-the-Art (SOTA) technique on a real-world data set.
10.1109/tccn.2026.3734985: Federated learning (FL) has become a promising paradigm for privacy-preserving and communication-efficient model training in vehicular networks. With the continuous expansion of vehicular networks, multiple FL tasks are often initiated concurrently by moving vehicles, which poses substantial challenges to the conventional single-task FL framework that relies on round-robin execution. Thus, effective vehicle scheduling is required to support concurrent participation in multiple FL tasks. Moreover, the straggler effect caused by vehicle heterogeneity can lead to inefficient resource utilization, as faster-training vehicles remain idle while waiting for slower ones. To address these challenges, we propose a distributed multi-task FL framework that enables independent and parallel execution of multiple FL tasks. A delay-driven hierarchical vehicle scheduling strategy is developed, which preferentially assigns vehicles with stronger training capabilities to tasks with more stringent latency requirements. To balance training latency and accuracy, we design a dynamic accuracy function, based on which a task utility function is defined. Subject to vehicle waiting-time constraints, we formulate a joint optimization problem that determines the number of global training rounds for each task, uplink bandwidth allocation, and vehicle CPU frequency to maximize the overall system utility. To solve it, we design a novel multi-agent twin-delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (MATD3)-based round-aware and resource optimization algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly improves system utility while reducing total energy consumption compared with baseline methods.
10.1109/tce.2026.3735776: Collaborative learning systems in resource-limited edge networks provide a privacy-preserving paradigm; however, regulations such as the “Right to be Forgotten” require Federated Unlearning (FU) to remove the influence of specific data. Existing FU research primarily focuses on efficiency, while security risks during distributed unlearning–particularly the performance recovery phase–remain less examined. Conventional backdoor attacks often rely on static triggers that may be weakened by unlearning. We propose LURA, a dynamic attack framework that exploits the unlearning-recovery procedure to reintroduce persistent backdoor behavior. Rather than resisting unlearning, the adversary requests removal to trigger recovery. LURA uses a Shadow Dataset to construct a Dynamic Legitimate Template that estimates locally acceptable update characteristics without a global view. It further uses a Cancellation Gradient that combines a recovery-aligned component with a dormant malicious component. This design enables the backdoor to be reactivated during recovery under the evaluated threat model. Across the four dataset/model settings in Table I, after unlearning and the specified 14-round recovery procedure, LURA improves post-unlearning attack success rate (P-ASR) by 42.26 percentage points and main-task accuracy (ACC) by 0.51 percentage points, on average, over the best listed static-backdoor baseline for each metric. Gradient Stealthiness Score (GSS) is used as a relative update-alignment measure. These findings suggest that FU security should consider both deletion and subsequent recovery stages.
10.1109/tce.2026.3735750: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across networked clients without centralizing raw data, yet faces challenges in server-side communication load and statistical heterogeneity. As FL deployments scale to hundreds or thousands of clients, the central-server uplink becomes a critical bottleneck while non-IID data distributions degrade convergence. This paper presents FedCluster, a hierarchical federated learning framework addressing these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms: (i) gradient-signature-based dynamic clustering that groups clients by training behavior, (ii) a Proxy Validation Unit (PVU) that filters biased or adversarial updates using fairness-aware weighting, and (iii) a two-level aggregation scheme reducingcentral-server uplinkcommunication fromO(Nd)toO(Kd)per round. Unlike existing clustered FL methods relying on static partitioning, FedCluster adapts client-cluster assignments dynamically based on training signatures. On the supervised CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 experiments under severe non-IID conditions (Dirichletα= 0.1), FedCluster improves accuracy by approximately 6 percentage points over FedAvg with stable convergence; the ablation attributes this gain jointly to an enhanced cluster-specific architecture and to dynamic clustering. On the HAR and MHEALTH activity benchmarks, evaluated separately as unsupervised federated clustering with simulated clients, the label-free variant FedCluster–U attains the highest ARI on MHEALTH and is competitive on HAR; these clustering results are not part of the +6-point claim. The server-uplink reduction is not an end-to-end saving: total communication is about 1.2× that of FedAvg, training time is 67% longer, and peak memory is 1.8×, an overhead that is justified when the server link, rather than client bandwidth or device resources, is the binding constraint. These results validate that hierarchical restructuring with fairness-aware validation provides a practical path toward robust federated learning with substantially reduced server-side communication.
10.1109/taes.2026.3733921: The evolution of low Earth orbit satellite constellations demands artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks that reconcile decentralized intelligence with extreme energy constraints. This article presents AstraFL—a federated learning paradigm for orbital edge computing that fundamentally rethinks model coordination through three conceptual innovations. First, we introduce a hybrid consensus architecture merging gossip-based peer-to-peer synchronization with blockchain-secured validation, enabling autonomous model aggregation across dynamic intersatellite networks without ground station dependencies. This dual-layer coordination mechanism establishes trust through probabilistically verified transactions while maintaining sublinear communication scaling. Second, we develop dynamic Block Minifloat arithmetic with hardware-algorithmic co-design, implementing adaptive precision scaling that automatically optimizes bit-width allocation across model training phases. This approach fundamentally rebalances the energy–accuracy trade space through layerwise quantization sensitivity analysis and radiation-hardened field programmable gate array (FPGA) acceleration. Third, the framework pioneers task-parallel federated updates through decomposed aggregation primitives, enabling simultaneous intraplane model merging and cross-plane gradient validation. Experimental validation across orbital hardware testbeds demonstrates how these architectural innovations collectively resolve the decentralization–security–efficiency trilemma: maintaining 98.7% model fidelity with 3.5× energy reduction versus FP32 baselines while achieving Byzantine fault tolerance through our stochastic proof-of-stake protocol. By redefining the coordination mechanisms and numerical foundations of spaceborne AI, AstraFL establishes an improved paradigm for autonomous learning in next-generation satellite constellations.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3737783: Federated Recommendation (FedRec) systems en able decentralized training of personalized recommendation models to mitigate privacy concerns. However, recent studies reveal their vulnerability to interaction-level membership in ference attacks. Existing attacks, such as IMIA, rely on the unrealistic assumption of knowing the system's negative sampling ratio, limiting their practicality. In this work, we propose T LiRA, a knowledge-free inference framework that exploits the intrinsic correlation between the optimization trajectory and interaction labels. T-LiRA eliminates the dependency on prior knowledge via a novel “propose-and-verify” paradigm. It first performs a coarse-grained clustering of item updates to establish a global context, followed by a fine-grained, item-wise two tailed likelihood ratio test. This test evaluates the directional alignment between the real item updates and simulated updates generated under conflicting label hypotheses. By focusing on the direction rather than the magnitude of updates, T-LiRA achieves robust inference even in the presence of clustering noise or varying gradient scales. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that T-LiRA achieves a 2× higher F1 score compared to state-of-the-art methods in knowledge-free settings and remains effective against defenses such as Local Differential Privacy (LDP) and regularization.
10.1109/tce.2026.3737469: The rapid growth of latency-sensitive applications, particularly within consumer electronics, has accelerated the adoption of edge–cloud computing, yet dynamic bandwidth allocation remains a persistent challenge for delivering robust quality of service (QoS) in mobile edge environments. Existing approaches often rely on centralized control, optimize isolated performance metrics, and fail to align user QoS requirements with provider incentives. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Utility-oriented Bandwidth Allocation via Auction Mechanisms (UBAAM), a decentralized framework that integrates auction-theoretic modeling, QoS-aware resource orchestration, and federated learning. UBAAM employs a multi-dimensional utility formulation and a dual-price adjustment mechanism to balance user demand and provider profitability. At the same time, a Lyapunov optimization-based equilibrium ensures system stability under time-varying workloads. A privacy-preserving federated learning module further enhances bid prediction accuracy without sharing sensitive data, and a priority-aware auction supports multi-class bandwidth allocation. Experimental results on a real-world edge–cloud platform show that UBAAM improves bandwidth utilization by 14%-33%, reduces carbon emissions by 19.4%, increases provider revenue by 88.5%, and lowers user costs by 31.9%, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving QoS, resource efficiency, and economic sustainability.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3737460: Federated Learning (FL), although designed to protect raw data privacy, remains vulnerable to model poisoning attacks due to its reliance on client-provided model updates. However, existing poisoning methods typically require access to client-side information or rely on restrictive assumptions, limiting their practicality in realistic, data-constrained environments. This raises the need for adaptive and data-free poisoning strategies that operate without access to client data. In this work, we introduce FedFree, a data-free model poisoning framework that requires only the sequence of server-broadcast global parameters. Its core is a history-guided inversion mechanism: FedFree estimates benign update statistics from the public global-model trajectory and shapes malicious updates that approximate benign client dynamics, reinforced by multi-source perturbation injection and an adaptive norm-clipping controller. Within its benign-update simulator, a block-wise, Shampoo-style second-order preconditioner is adopted as a numerical-stability enhancement rather than the primary source of attack effectiveness. Extensive experiments across three datasets and eleven aggregation strategies (including the FedAvg no-defense baseline) show that, under sustained adversarial participation, FedFree delivers the strongest degradation among all compared attacks under Multi-Krum, Trimmed-mean, and FLShield, ranks second or third under FedAvg, CC, RFA, RoFL, and FedGT, and is most strongly suppressed by the similarity- and projection-based defenses FoolsGold and DnC. We further analyze the quality of the generated benign simulation module. The surrogate updates exhibit high statistical consistency with real client updates, achieving cosine similarity above 0.993 and norm ratios close to 1.0 under different data heterogeneity settings. Ablation studies further show that history/trajectory modeling is the dominant driver of attack effectiveness, while the Shampoo-style design mainly improves numerical stability while preserving overall attack behavior.
10.1109/tcomm.2026.3738508: Federated learning (FL) facilitates knowledge interaction among agents (both spatially and temporally) by keeping raw data on-device and exchanging only model updates, thereby improving localization performance for multi-agent systems. However, existing FL-based localization models typically lack the capability to capture agent-specific features and require substantial computation and communication resources, limiting their effectiveness and widespread adoption. To address these challenges, we propose a lightweight personalized federated learning (LPFL) approach for spatial and temporal multi-agent interactive localization (MAIL). Specifically, each agent maintains a local localization model while the central server manages a global one. During each round, agents adapt the broadcast global model with local training data, compute validation gradients, and upload them for server aggregation. This validation-guided update enables LPFL to enhance both personalization and cross-agent generalization, improving cooperative localization accuracy. Additionally, adaptive model pruning and gradient quantization are implemented to compress the model, aiming at improving the computational and communication efficiencies for multi-agent systems. Theoretical analyses validate the training performance and efficiency of LPFL, making it a feasible and reliable framework for MAIL. Finally, we conduct comprehensive real-world experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of LPFL.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3738968: The increasing deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) applications has created a growing need for distributed learning frameworks that can operate efficiently across resource-constrained edge environments while preserving data privacy. Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data. However, its communication overhead, computational burden, and limited scalability make it less suitable for large-scale hierarchical edge networks. In this paper, we propose Hierarchical Federated Split Learning (HFSL), a unified (UAV)-assisted edge-fog-cloud framework that combines the complementary strengths of FL and Split Learning (SL) to improve communication efficiency, scalability, and privacy. HFSL introduces activation similarity-based clustering and spatio-temporal activation filtering to reduce redundant communication, adaptive UAV altitude optimization to improve wireless connectivity under dynamic network conditions, and a privacy-preserving training strategy based on Differential Privacy (DP) and activation-level leakage mitigation. Extensive experiments across eight image and tabular benchmark datasets demonstrate that HFSL outperforms state-of-the-art FL and SL methods on the more challenging heterogeneous benchmarks, reducing energy consumption by up to 50%, training latency by 40%, and communication overhead by 35%, while improving classification accuracy by up to 6%. These results show that HFSL provides an effective and scalable distributed learning framework for next-generation UAV-assisted edge networks.
10.1109/tce.2026.3738403: Connected and autonomous consumer vehicles face escalating cybersecurity threats as their attack surfaces expand through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication, over-the-air (OTA) updates, and complex electronic architectures. Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment (TARA), mandated by ISO/SAE 21434, is essential for systematic threat mitigation, yet many automated TARA pipelines still rely on tree-structured threat models that fail to capture shared attack paths, on rule-based or LLM-driven reasoning without graph-structural learning, and on black-box risk scoring that lacks the traceability expected for safety-critical systems. Attack-graph–based automotive TARA has been studied for more than a decade (e.g., MulVAL, CarVal, GAPP, THREATGET); our contribution is not to introduce attack graphs to this area, but to integrateunifiedgraph construction, multi-task Graph Attention Network (GAT) inference, and a layered explanation mechanism into a single learnable pipeline. In this paper, we propose AG-TARA, which combines attack graph modeling, Graph Attention Networks (GAT), and a three-level explainable AI architecture for automotive cybersecurity assessment: it first constructs a unified attack graph from vehicle configuration data, vulnerability databases, and standardized attack pattern repositories to enable node sharing and edge reuse across threat scenarios; a multi-head GAT-based risk inference engine then learns structural attack patterns for simultaneous node risk classification and attack path prediction; finally, a three-level explainability architecture combining attention weight visualization, GNNExplainer-based feature attribution, and attack path contribution analysis provides traceable risk explanations aligned with the auditability principles of ISO/SAE 21434. Extensive experiments on a real-world automotive cybersecurity dataset demonstrate that AG-TARA achieves 82.35% accuracy and 0.8367 Macro-F1 in risk classification and 0.9873 AUC in attack path prediction, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art GNN and LLM-based baselines while reducing per-scenario analysis time by over 97% compared to LLM-agent methods. We additionally outline a federated AG-TARA deployment mode and report a small-scale FedAvg experiment as a preliminary validation; full federated deployment remains future work.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3739043: Recent advancements in Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) have introduced a transformative approach, enabling organizations with limited and fragmented datasets to collaboratively train machine learning models and enhance data utility. Meanwhile, the tightening of global data privacy regulations-driven by heightened concerns over data breaches and information leakage-has spurred the development of numerous privacy-preserving VFL frameworks. Among these, boosting algorithms have emerged as particularly promising due to their flexibility and wide-ranging applicability. Although several privacy-preserving approaches to Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost) have been investigated, AdaBoost training specifically within the VFL framework remains largely underexplored. Furthermore, existing VFL solutions based on tree-boosting methods often exhibit suboptimal performance when adapted to the AdaBoost paradigm. To address this gap, we propose an efficient and privacy-preserving AdaBoost training framework for VFL. Our approach introduces a packing technique based on symmetric homomorphic encryption (SHE) to reduce communication overhead. Additionally, we design secure sub-protocols for batch data comparison and minimum value computation, enabling confidential generation of prediction labels and the secure selection of the optimal weak classifier in each training round. These components collectively form the foundation of our VFL AdaBoost training framework. Our security analysis confirms that our scheme ensures privacy guarantees under the honest-but-curious model. Experimental evaluations further demonstrate that our framework not only achieves high accuracy, but also maintains superior computational and communication efficiency when compared to existing baseline methods.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3739050: Federated Recommender Systems (FedRecs) have gained significant traction as a privacy-preserving paradigm, enabling the collaborative training of global models without exchanging raw user data. Despite these advancements, standard FedRec models remain susceptible to attribute inference attacks, where adversaries can exploit shared embeddings to recover sensitive demographic information such as gender and race. To mitigate this risk, we propose targeting these specific features through federated unlearning. We introduce Aegis, a novel post-training framework designed to selectively purge sensitive attributes from user embeddings, thereby thwarting inference attacks while preserving recommendation utility. Technically, Aegis leverages embedding disentanglement to separate sensitive features from general preference information, using an information-theoretic multi-component loss function to optimize the balance between privacy protection and model performance. Crucially, our framework is capable of operating without access to original training interaction data through autonomous client-side protection. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Aegis effectively safeguards user privacy with minimal degradation in recommendation accuracy.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3739774: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across multiple parties without sharing raw local data, and has been widely deployed in healthcare, finance, and in dustrial IoT scenarios. Existing privacy-preserving FL methods mainly rely on differential privacy, secure aggregation, and homomorphic encryption, offering diverse degrees of defense against gradient leakage and model-inversion attacks. However, in practical edge deployments, rational, resource-constrained clients may intentionally cut down local training efforts. Such client behavior slows convergence, hurts model performance, and raises cumulative system costs throughout training. Furthermore, prevailing privacy mechanisms introduce non-negligible computational and communication overhead, which aggravates energy consumption. To resolve these issues and coordinate autonomous client decisions under privacy and resource constraints, we propose FedPGame, a potential game-based federated learning framework. Specifically, we model privacy-aware local strategy selection as a finite non-cooperative potential game, enabling clients to autonomously choose their resource-investment levels. We further devise a heterogeneity-aware client-level cost function together with its corresponding global potential function. This design aligns unilateral client-side cost reduction with global potential descent and guarantee convergence to a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Differential privacy is incorporated through an explicit training-horizon (ε,δ)-DP upper bound and a pre scribed DP-budget constraint. Solid theoretical analysis and comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that FedPGame achieves a favorable trade-off among privacy protection, client autonomy, model utility, and energy efficiency.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3739767: With the increasing demand for privacy and distributed data compliance, federated learning (FL) has become a promising paradigm for collaborative network traffic classification (NTC) without sharing raw traffic data. However, real-world network environments are inherently open, where the emergence of new applications and unknown attacks introduces open-set challenges. To ensure service quality and network security, models need not only to classify known traffic classes accurately but also to identify unknown ones. Despite recent efforts to extend FL to Open-Set NTC (OSNTC), most current FL methods are still confined to the closed-set assumption, leaving the challenge of Federated OSNTC (FedOSNTC) largely unresolved. Therefore, this paper proposes FedUTD, a novel Federated Unknown Traffic Detection framework that introduces: 1) multi-scale prefix truncation, a customized contrastive learning strategy that leverages multi-granularity traffic characteristics to enhance feature discriminability; 2) an improved federated communication mechanism that enriches the transmitted information through pseudo-sample generation to mitigate data heterogeneity while retaining substantially lower communication cost; and 3) a lightweight dual-layer OSNTC approach designed to reduce local training and inference overhead during local unknown-traffic detection. Extensive experiments on four real-world network traffic datasets demonstrate that FedUTD consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving an F1 gain of 5–21%.
10.1109/tce.2026.3740729: Intelligent electric vehicles (EVs) are becoming high-value consumer electronic devices equipped with computation, sensing, and communication capabilities. However, using their idle vehicular computing capacity for federated intelligent services requires the simultaneous coordination of model architecture, hardware demand, owner incentives, and voluntary participation. These decisions are typically handled separately, which can lead to a mismatch between learning workloads and available resources and, consequently, unstable service provision. To address this problem, this paper proposes an architecture-aware dynamic matching and two-tier pricing framework that jointly considers model architecture, architecture-dependent hardware burden, owner response, and federated learning performance. Calibrated hardware profiles characterize device-specific latency, memory, communication, and energy demands; a Stackelberg pricing mechanism coordinates platform decisions with individually rational owner participation; and Hardware-Incentive-Coupled Evolutionary Federated Architecture Search (HIC-EvoFAS) performs feasibility-aware, multi-fidelity search over architecture and service decisions. The selected architecture reaches 89.12% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 93.78% on the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark (GTSRB). Compared with federated neural architecture search (FedNAS), it reduces communication volume and round latency by 17.11% and 12.78%, respectively, while the proposed pricing mechanism improves platform utility by 58.90% over fixed pricing without revenue sharing. These results show that incorporating hardware requirements and owner incentives directly into architecture selection can improve both federated learning performance and the practical use of distributed vehicular computing capacity resources.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3740920: Privacy-preserving federated learning commonly adopts secure aggregation to hide individual updates; however, secure aggregation alone does not guarantee that an untrusted aggregation server aggregates the intended set of clients correctly under dynamic membership. This work presents EVA, an efficient framework for privacy-preserving and verifiable aggregation in federated learning. EVA decouples masked-update aggregation from masking-secret aggregation. Clients conceal local updates via a subset-sum-based masking mechanism and upload masked updates together with lightweight checksums to the aggregation server, while sending the corresponding auxiliary masking secrets to a trusted execution environment (TEE), which aggregates them. The server aggregates only masked updates and checksums, whereas the TEE aggregates the auxiliary secrets into a single secret state. Given the server output and the TEE-provided aggregated secret state, the clients participating in the next round can recover the unmasked aggregate and verify a single global consistency relation that binds the result to the aggregated checksum, thereby detecting deviation from correct aggregation except with negligible probability. EVA further supports anonymous yet authenticated participation via time-bound group signatures, enabling revocation and accountable traceability when required. We implement EVA in Go and Python and evaluate it on MNIST with MLP and CNN models. Experimental results show that EVA achieves model accuracy comparable to that of FedAvg while incurring low per-round overheads: the aggregation server remains lightweight even for large models, and the TEE overhead stays moderate, yielding substantial efficiency gains over representative baselines.
10.1109/tce.2026.3740732: Drone delivery networks require authorization across fleet-operator and civil-aviation domains and protected federated learning (FL) exchanges over wireless links. Concurrent associations require endpoint-specific keys and efficient protection of shared payloads. We present SMVAKA, a simultaneous multi-vertiport authentication and key-agreement protocol built from established primitives. Two non-colluding clouds process target-specific Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) shares as additive components. Sender-specific secrets reach authorized vertiports through an ECCDH-masked authenticated Invertible Bloom Lookup Table. The intersection of both cloud decisions determines accepted associations, whose endpoints combine these components into distinct keys. Neither cloud reconstructs an end-point key. Established epoch secrets support one protected broad-cast payload per sender and FL round. A Real-or-Random analysis establishes fresh-session key indistinguishability and single-cloud privacy under honest-but-curious clouds, and Colored Petri Nets verify the finite-state protocol flow. In the evaluated work-loads, SMVAKA reduced sender-side protection operation counts by a factor of nine relative to the repeated-pairwise baseline, with mean terminal-accuracy differences within 0.03 percentage points. Two authenticated recovery attempts achieved 99.58% key reconstruction at 10% effective loss. The measured per-target broadcast-size slope differed from the analytical prediction by 0.7%.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3741858: Integrating Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into federated learning enables efficient distributed fine-tuning of large models, but introduces two key challenges: protecting client updates and ensuring correct aggregation under heterogeneous ranks. Existing solutions either degrade accuracy through differential privacy or incur high computational and communication overhead with encryption. This paper proposes HEFedLoRA, a privacy-preserving federated LoRA framework that combines alternating aggregation with a threshold Paillier cryptosystem to securely aggregate the active low-rank factor in each round without revealing additional information about individual client updates beyond what can be inferred from the released aggregate factors. HEFedLoRA also eliminates aggregation discordance while supporting heterogeneous client ranks through a shared upper-rank alignment mechanism. Theoretical analysis proves security under the semi-honest model. Experiments show that HEFedLoRA retains 99.47% of the plaintext baseline accuracy, reduces server aggregation runtime by up to 28.5× relative to Se cLoRA, and approximately halves the communication overhead compared with naive encrypted baselines.
10.1109/tpami.2026.3741546: Federated Graph Learning (FGL) enables privacy-preserving training of Graph Neural Networks across distributed clients but remains vulnerable to backdoor attacks that bias the global model through topology-aware manipulations. The key challenge is to disentangle benign heterogeneity from adversarial perturbations on graph structure. To address this, our conference version FedTGE proposed a core comprising Topological Energy Difference Clustering (TEDC)—instantiated via Meta Energy Calibration (MEC)—and Topological Energy Similarity Propagation (TESP), which builds an energy-similarity graph among trusted clients to modulate aggregation. However, distinguishing localized structural triggers from benign distribution shifts and performing reliable client attestation remained challenging. Therefore, this journal version extends our preliminary work to FedTGE++ by adding (i) Quantized Topological Prototype Purification (QTPP), which learns a discrete structural codebook to capture fine-grained triggers, and (ii) Dual-View Attestation Protocol (DVAP), which requires consensus between energy- and prototype-based GMM clustering. With the full four-component pipeline, this journal version further tackles two key challenges overlooked by energy-only defenses: (a) precise localization of subtle structural triggers under non-IID graphs via a discrete topological codebook, and (b) heterogeneity-aware attestation through cross-view consensus and topology-aware aggregation. We also broaden the reported experiments across datasets, triggers, malicious proportions, and non-IID regimes. Experiments on node-classification benchmarks show that FedTGE++ improves the accuracy–defense trade-off over the evaluated baselines under the tested threat model. The implementation and complete experiment configurations will be released upon publication.
10.1109/tcc.2026.3738056: As the next generation of digital frontier technology, metaverse renders an immersive experience for metaverse users via avatar. As a paradigm of distributed learning, federated learning (FL) facilitates metaverse users' collaborative training of the global model parameter, thereby promoting the metaverse experience. In practical edge-assisted deployments, metaverse intelligence must be delivered under connectivity and resource constraints such as intermittent access, heterogeneous devices, and edge–cloud resource limitations. However, the existing FL algorithms fail to reflect the feature of metaverse, such as dynamic data updating. To make the FL framework closer to the characteristics of the metaverse scenario, we propose a novel personalized FL algorithm, and its originalities are delineated by the following aspects: (1) Users are stringently classified and more nuanced treating in the gradient iterative calculation with gradient sparsification; (2) The personalized FL algorithm considers knowledge transfer toward learning from the pertinent metaverse users, in which the KL difference function is used to calculate the difference between model parameters and hence adaptively reinforce the collaboration among metaverse users with small data heterogeneity; (3) The update strategy of local private data and public data is designed so that the latest updated data is involved in the next episode; (4) Hosting model parameter is defined to knowledge transfer with predicted knowledge coefficient matrix, and it also used to host avatar when the metaverse user is offline. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed FL algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art FL algorithms on both the MNIST, FMNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. We have opened sourced our code in https://github.com/zhulinlijs/Fed learning.
10.1109/tcss.2026.3736859: Federated learning (FL) is an emerging distributed machine learning (ML) technique that addresses data privacy concerns by enabling multiple edge devices (EDs) to train a global model while keeping the data decentralized. Despite the advantages, FL faces significant challenges, such as data heterogeneity and slower convergence rates. Conventional FL uses plain gradient descent and momentum-based gradient descent for training models on the EDs, with simple averaging at intervals to update the global model. However, there is limited research on the Nesterov accelerated gradient (NAG) in FL, despite its recognized ability to achieve faster convergence than standard momentum. Motivated by this, we propose a new federated learning with weighted averaging and Nesterov momentum (FedWAN), which combines NAG for model training on the EDs with a weighted averaging method to handle data heterogeneity and update the global model. The weights are calculated using the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the local data distributions and an aggregated global distribution, prioritizing EDs with more diverse data. The performance of the proposed method is examined through extensive simulations on benchmark datasets, and it is observed that the convergence rate on non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data improves by 3%–12% compared to existing Momentum-FL solutions and by approximately 1.5–2$\mathbf{\times}$compared to Non-IID targeted FL solutions.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3742206: Trajectory anomaly detection is increasingly used for safety auditing and operational monitoring in modern urban transportation systems (e.g., taxi and ride-hailing services). The massive volume of trajectory data and the demand for reliable analytics require scalable storage and computation, which are commonly supported by cloud platforms. However, practical deployment still faces two major challenges. One is the privacy challenge caused by data outsourcing, since personal mobility traces and anomaly detection results are highly sensitive. The other is the efficiency challenge introduced by privacy-preserving computation. Trajectory anomalies may occur at different granularities, including unusual origin or destination points and abnormal route deviations, while cryptographic operations make fine-grained trajectory analytics costly. As a result, existing privacy-preserving designs often face difficulty balancing detection reliability, interpretability, and efficiency at scale. To address these challenges, we present PFATD, a privacy-preserving multi-tier anomaly detection framework for federated trajectories in an outsourced two-Cloud non-collusion model, which provides interpretable deviation signals for anomaly auditing under privacy constraints. PFATD improves scalability and preserves trajectory confidentiality via secret sharing (SS), combining lightweight critical-point candidate filtering with computation-friendly secure path-level analytics, and privacy-preserving risk-score fusion. We provide a simulation-based security analysis, showing that our scheme is secure against honest-but-curious, non-colluding Clouds. We further evaluate PFATD on real-world datasets, and extensive experimental results demonstrate that it achieves both high accuracy and practical efficiency under privacy constraints.
10.1109/tnse.2026.3742774: 5G-Advanced (5G-A) networks are evolving into intelligent coordination platforms for massive AI agents, including large-model-enabled devices, edge services, robots, vehicles, and network-side autonomous functions. These agents need to collaboratively adapt models and exchange knowledge without centralizing raw data, making federated learning (FL) a natural mechanism for distributed model evolution. However, compromised or malfunctioning agents may launch Byzantine attacks by uploading manipulated updates, thereby corrupting the shared model and weakening trustworthy coordination. Existing Byzantine-resilient FL defenses mainly rely on robust aggregation rules under the canonical star architecture, leaving the role of network-agent topology largely underexplored. This paper proposes FedTGR, a topology-guided grouping framework for Byzantine-resilient federated learning among massive AI agent clients. FedTGR overlays a virtual group topology on participating agent clients, filters suspicious updates through plug-in robust aggregation rules at a coordinator server, and enforces intra-group and inter-group model alignment through an ADMM-based consensus mechanism. By adjusting the number of groups, FedTGR reshapes the coordination topology and suppresses residual Byzantine influence while preserving the standard client-server FL workflow. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and FEMNIST show that FedTGR improves test accuracy under diverse poisoning attacks and aggregation rules; a three-run ablation further shows reduced final-accuracy variability for the complete framework. These results support topology-guided coordination as a practical learning-layer mechanism for trustworthy federated model evolution in 5G-A autonomous agent systems.
10.1109/tsp.2026.3742745: Efficient communication is crucial for decentralized optimization and learning to scale effectively in large-scale engineered systems. Although performing multiple local updates per communication round significantly enhances communication efficiency in server-assisted distributed learning (i.e., federated learning), extending this strategy to fully decentralized settings remains a fundamental challenge. In fact, to incorporate multiple local updates, existing decentralized methods often rely on small/diminishing stepsizes, sacrifice consensus guarantees, or incur high communication overhead due to auxiliary variable exchanges. In this paper, we propose MIND, a fully decentralized algorithm that overcomes these limitations and is applicable to both exact and stochastic gradient scenarios. MIND introduces a novel update mechanism that guarantees convergence without auxiliary variables, exchanging only a single vector between two interacting agents per communication round. This reduces communication costs by at least half compared to existing methods, which require sharing both the optimization and auxiliary variables. Additionally, MIND achieves accurate convergence with a network-independent stepsize, unlike most existing decentralized optimization methods where each agent must access global network information to determine the stepsize. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MIND outperforms existing methods in both convergence speed and communication efficiency.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3742261: The Internet of Things (IoT) forms the foundation of modern smart environments, enabling intelligent industries, homes, cities, healthcare, and autonomous systems. However, as IoT devices increasingly connect to cloud platforms and the Internet, they become highly vulnerable to network intrusions that can lead to critical data breaches and service disruptions. This paper proposes a Contrastive Federated Semi-Supervised Learning Network Intrusion Detection framework (CFedSSL-NID), specifically tailored to enhance the security of IoT communications. It addresses practical scenarios where clients lack labeled data and computational resources, and where data privacy is paramount. The CFedSSL-NID framework enhances detection performance and robustness. It uniquely achieves this by synergistically leveraging abundant, unlabeled data from distributed IoT gateways through self-supervised contrastive learning, while optimally integrating supervised signals from a central server. This dual approach enables highly accurate intrusion detection while substantially mitigating the reliance on scarce and costly labeled data. Experiments on the TON-IoT, UNSW-NB15, and NSL-KDD datasets show that CFedSSL-NID outperforms federated and centralized baselines; additional evaluations under Non-IID data, asynchronous participation, and malicious-client updates confirm robustness, while communication and edge-inference analyses indicate its deployment feasibility.
10.1109/tccn.2026.3741950: Federated learning (FL) can effectively enable multiple distributed devices to collaboratively train a global model without sharing raw data, offering strong data privacy protection and scalability for the Internet of Things (IoT). However, FL typically requires a large amount of labeled data to achieve global model convergence, which limits its applicability in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a semi-supervised federated learning (SSFL) framework for uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-enabled surveillance systems. Each UAV collects unlabeled surveillance data and trains a local model by adopting both pre-stored labeled data and newly collected unlabeled data. To minimize the total completion time of the SSFL process, we first analyze the correlation between the convergence of the global model and the volume of unlabeled data. We further reveal a tradeoff between the number of communication rounds and the per-round training latency. Moreover, we derive that there exists an optimal oblique photography (OP) angle for UAV-based data collection, which simultaneously improves image resolution and reduces the transmission latency. These findings highlight the unique interplay between sensing geometry and communication efficiency, which has been largely overlooked in previous works. Finally, we jointly optimize the UAV position, OP angle, unlabeled data volume, resource allocation, and number of communication rounds to minimize the SSFL completion time in a multi-UAV network. Simulation results show that compared with existing benchmarks, the proposed scheme significantly reduces training time and accelerates convergence speed. Moreover, our results reveal two key tradeoffs: (1) the amount of unlabeled data must balance local computation delay against global convergence gain, and (2) the OP angle governs image fidelity and transmission efficiency, reflecting the intrinsic linkage between sensing and communication design.
10.1109/tnse.2026.3742943: With the rapid expansion of edge devices, federated learning (FL) has emerged as a critical paradigm for enabling collaborative intelligence while preserving data privacy. However, deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained edge hardware remains challenging due to high computational and energy demands. To address this, we propose a novel quantum-inspired neuromorphic federated learning framework, called FL-quantum leaky integrate-and-fire (FL-QLIF). At the core of our approach is an enhanced QLIF neuron model that utilizes quantum rotation gates to simulate synaptic integration and membrane potential leakage simultaneously, offering a mathematically robust and computationally efficient alternative to traditional activation functions. We rigorously validate the framework through extensive experiments, demonstrating that its convergence behavior closely aligns with theoretical predictions regarding learning rates and local update steps. Extensive experiments on MNIST, KMNIST, and FashionMNIST datasets demonstrate that FL-QLIF achieves test accuracy comparable to classical artificial neural networks (ANNs) while significantly outperforming standard variational quantum neural networks (QNNs), particularly in statistically heterogeneous (non-iid) environments. Furthermore, our energy analysis reveals that the proposed framework delivers substantial efficiency gains, reducing energy consumption by$4.4\times$to$10\times$compared to ANN baselines. Finally, we validate the system's scalability, showing robust performance even under low client participation rates (10%), establishing FL-QLIF as a viable solution for sustainable, privacy-preserving edge intelligence.
10.1109/tce.2026.3742394: With the rapid proliferation of smart consumer electronics (CE) such as wearables, smart home hubs, and Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled medical devices, in-home health monitoring has become increasingly important with the growth of the aging population. Machine Learning (ML) has been widely applied in this domain, enabling intelligent functions in consumer-grade health devices and enhancing user experience. However, existing Centralized Learning (CL) approaches face critical challenges of data privacy and communication overhead, limiting real-world applicability. To address these challenges, we proposeProxyHome, a cloud–edge-based Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) framework for in-home health monitoring. The framework is designed for deployment on everyday CE platforms (e.g., smartphones, wearables, and smart sensors) that form part of modern IoT-based health ecosystems. ProxyHome introducesPersonalized Proxy Models(PPMs), which distill knowledge from local models to enable personalization while protecting user privacy. These lightweight PPMs are used for on-device inference and are never exchanged, ensuring communication efficiency and scalability. Meanwhile, ProxyHome exchanges Encoder/Decoder components frequently to support generalization, while the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) is exchanged less often with Differential Privacy (DP) to maintain personalization. To handle imbalanced and Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (Non-IID) data, ProxyHome integrates a lightweight generative convolutional autoencoder (GCAE) that compresses and reconstructs sensor data, maintaining accuracy while reducing communication costs. Extensive experiments on a human activity dataset demonstrate that ProxyHome achieves superior communication efficiency and competitive accuracy compared with state-of-the-art methods, including FedHome and FedProx. These results validate ProxyHome as a robust, privacy-preserving, and communication-efficient solution for scalable in-home health monitoring across consumer IoT and smart healthcare electronics.
10.1109/tcsvt.2026.3742509: Federated continual learning (FCL) is an emerging distributed learning framework that enables multiple edge clients to collaboratively and incrementally train a shared server-side model on evolving task streams while ensuring data privacy. In this setting, the server-side model is required to continuously adapt to new tasks while simultaneously retaining knowledge acquired from old tasks. However, FCL suffers from two fundamental challenges: catastrophic forgetting, where newly learned knowledge overwrites previously acquired knowledge, and classification space entanglement, where decision boundaries across tasks become progressively overlapped, leading to significant performance degradation. To address these challenges, we propose ReKAN, an effective FCL method that integrates an experience replay strategy with a task-adaptive classifier. Specifically, we propose a replay strategy based on reducible loss (ReLoss) to identify and retain important historical samples under strict memory constraints, thereby improving knowledge retention for previously learned tasks. In addition, we replace the conventional Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)-based classifier with a task-adaptive classifier inspired by the Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN), which enables localized model updates and mitigates the disruption of established decision boundaries across tasks. Extensive experiments conducted on widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that ReKAN achieves state-of-the-art performance in FCL, highlighting its effectiveness in resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive environments.
10.1109/tii.2026.3737474: Wind turbine fault diagnosis is crucial for reducing operational and maintenance costs, but existing federated learning frameworks suffer from model performance degradation, unfair distribution, and insufficient generalization. To address these issues, we propose a fairness-enhanced federated learning framework, named FEFedWT, for wind turbine fault diagnosis, which alleviates the two-stage decoupling issue between contribution assessment and reward allocation in existing methods. First, embedding the sharpness-aware minimization optimizer, which seeks flat minima on the loss surface to reduce model convergence fluctuations and performance degradation. Second, proposing a dynamic contribution assessment mechanism that integrates regularization with exponential weighted averaging, enabling real-time evaluation of wind farm contributions. Third, designing a hierarchical gradient pruning algorithm combined with contribution-driven mask generation to prioritize retaining effective gradients from high-contribution wind farms thereby ensuring fairness. Theoretical analysis is performed to prove the fairness of the proposed framework. Extensive experiments on real wind turbine datasets demonstrate the superiority of the FEFedWT framework, achieving an accuracy of 96.34% and a Jain fairness index of 98.98%, respectively, in terms of diagnostic performance and fairness.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3743397: Edge intelligence-enabled Internet of Things (Edge-IoT) increasingly relies on decentralized on-device learning to reduce cloud dependence and keep locally collected IoT data on terminal devices. However, deployed models may still memorize privacy-sensitive class-level knowledge and must support deletion requests after training. This paper studies class-level federated unlearning in a serverless Edge-IoT workflow where each IoT client maintains a sparse personalized IoT-local model and exchanges model information only with neighbors. We propose DeSPU, a decentralized sparse personalized federated unlearning framework under a practical deletion-window protocol. DeSPU estimates a target-class direction with a lightweight dual-model mechanism, applies semantic-layer adaptive linear unlearning to suppress target knowledge, and performs topology-aware local repair regularized by cached neighbor snapshots collected during routine peer-to-peer training. The online unlearning path does not store historical gradients and does not introduce additional post-request model communication beyond routine decentralized exchanges; the one-time$\beta $calibration scan is reported separately, and the calibrated$\beta $can be reused under the same configuration. To propagate deletion status beyond the requester, DeSPU also attaches a metadata-only forgetting flag to those routine exchanges and invalidates affected cached neighbor References at receiving clients. Experiments on CIFAR-10, MNIST, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10 show near-zero target-class accuracy with high retained accuracy, up to$\sim 4.7\times 10^{3}$speedup over full retraining on CIFAR-10, and membership-inference ROC-AUC close to random guessing. Additional analyses over seeds, requester clients, target classes, cache staleness, sparsity, communication, and hardware cost further demonstrate the practicality and limitations of DeSPU for privacy-compliant Edge-IoT deployments. The project link is available athttps://github.com/aaaM2002/UN_CODE
10.1109/tce.2026.3744254: Vision-language model (VLM) agents are entering smart-home consumer electronics such as hubs, cameras and connected appliances, where a single hallucinated action, for example turning on a stove mistaken for a microwave, can cause damage or a safety incident. Across five open-weight VLMs from four families (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, Phi-3.5-Vision, PaliGemma) and three parameter scales (3B, 4B, 7B), zero-shot accuracy with two-shot text prompts stays below 73% on our test splits. This paper makes four contributions. First, we build SmartHome-VSV, a benchmark of 22,841 training samples and three test splits (GQA-test, HARD-CONF, ADE-CONF) auto-derived from public scene graphs with no human annotation. Second, we propose a Confidence-Aware Selective Tree-of-Thoughts verifier with three branches, a JSON five-tuple verdict (C), a full-image yes/no detector (A) and a bounding-box yes/no detector (B), trained jointly by multi-task LoRA so that a soft threshold on the single-token logprobs of A and B routes the final decision. Third, we deploy the verifier under FFA-LoRA federated fine-tuning across three non-IID households and confirm that aggregation is exact to machine precision. Fourth, the same mechanism reduces dangerous error by only 2.8 percentage points under centralized training, yet recovers 28.2 points (37% relative) under federated drift, a ten-fold amplification. Threshold sweeps, calibration analysis across all backbones, branch ablations, bootstrap confidence intervals, latency measurements and robustness tests show that the gain is statistically reliable and adds only about 4% inference latency. Confidence-Aware Selective ToT therefore acts as a distributional-robustness safety net for federated generative AI on consumer devices.
10.1109/tvt.2026.3744590: Large-scale Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations offer a promising substrate for in-network intelligence, but their rapid orbital motion makes it difficult to sustain geographically meaningful collaborative learning over a fixed region of interest (ROI). A satellite group that is initially well aligned with a target region will continuously drift as satellites move, which complicates both participant maintenance and inter-satellite model propagation. To address this challenge, we proposeSkyAnchor, an ROI-anchored decentralized learning framework for ISL-enabled LEO constellations. SkyAnchor couples two key components: 1) an ROI-anchored block-maintenance mechanism that keeps a fixed-cardinality satellite block geographically aligned with the target region through shape-preserving, timer-gated, and delay-aware anchor shifts, and 2) a block-based decentralized federated learning scheme that performs collaborative training over the maintained block via ISL model propagation and fully-connected logical aggregation with consensus momentum. We further provide a convergence characterization of the resulting learning dynamics under the fully-connected aggregation rule. The proposed framework offers a practical way to jointly support geographic service persistence and collaborative intelligence in dynamic LEO satellite networks.
10.1109/tvt.2026.3744546: In wireless federated learning scenarios, the heterogeneity of transmission conditions and limited communication resources bring challenges to the efficient exchange of parameters. To address the issue, we propose a joint allocation scheme of quantization bits, bandwidth, and client scheduling for model parameter updating. Considering the effects of quantization and wireless transmission, we first derive an upper bound on the error of the global aggregation model as the optimization objective, and then formulate an optimization problem of quantization bits, bandwidth allocation, and client scheduling under the constraints of total bandwidth and channel capacity. Since the problem is non-convex with coupled variables, we decompose it into two subproblems by the alternating optimization method. In the first subproblem, we derive the closed-form solution of the optimal quantization bits based on the KKT conditions. The second subproblem, concerning the bandwidth allocation and client scheduling variable, is a feasibility problem. The experimental results show that the proposed algorithm yields a better model accuracy than the baseline method in both IID and non-IID partitions. Furthermore, the accuracy improvement is significant in the non-IID partition.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3744708: Federated learning (FL), as a distributed machine learning paradigm, enables multiple clients to collaboratively optimize a shared model with a cloud server (CS) without sharing raw data. However, a resource-constrained CS may produce inaccurate global models, while Byzantine adversaries can compromise aggregation, threatening the reliability and robustness of FL. To address these issues, we propose VBDPFL, a verifiable and Byzantine-robust differentially private FL scheme. Specifically, VBDPFL provides threefold protection: 1) it employs differential privacy (DP) to protect local gradients, coupled with gradient correction that partially offsets DP-induced noise bias; 2) it introduces a multi-penalty trust score for client reliability assessment and suspicion-based aggregation with adaptive threshold for dynamic identification and filtering of malicious updates; 3) it builds an efficient bilinear pairing-based verifiable aggregation protocol to ensure the correctness of global models. Theoretical analysis provides guarantees for convergence, gradient correction, privacy, security, and computational complexity. Extensive experiments show that VBDPFL remains accurate and practical under multiple state-of-the-art Byzantine attacks.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3744677: In the context of federated learning, when a participant needs to withdraw from collaboration for specific reasons, it should have the right to completely remove its relevant data from the global model. Additionally, if a malicious party executes a poisoning attack, its harmful data must be removed from the global model. To achieve this, we propose a client-level federated unlearning method with asymptotic optimization (FedAOP), which effectively eliminates the influence of client data, maintains model accuracy, and avoids catastrophic forgetting. This method also introduces a calculation for the optimal unlearning round based on data influence, thereby balancing storage and communication costs. And by randomly initializing certain specific layers, the unlearning process is accelerated. We further assess the effectiveness of unlearning by introducing membership inference and data poisoning attacks during training. Experiments on the MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our method is both effective and efficient.
10.1109/tbdata.2026.3744818: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for privacy-preserving distributed machine learning. Decentralized FL (DFL), by removing reliance on a single global coordinator, offers enhanced robustness, scalability, and autonomy. However, this architecture introduces challenges in communication, optimization, and security. This survey provides a structured synthesis of DFL, spanning its theoretical foundations, communication and optimization mechanisms, privacy and trust protection, application paradigms, and implementation platforms. We first establish the theoretical framework of DFL through algebraic graph theory and decentralized learning principles. Next, we investigate optimization strategies for data heterogeneity and communication bottlenecks through methodological categorization. Additionally, we analyze privacy threats in decentralized systems and present solutions ranging from differential privacy to cryptographic techniques. We investigate each dimension by reviewing established techniques and discussing their pros and cons, as well as the unresolved challenges. Moreover, we introduce the application scenarios and software frameworks of DFL. Finally, we outline future research directions. In a nutshell, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the fundamentals of DFL, its applications in edge computing and multi-agent systems, and the existing challenges and open issues with insights for future in-depth research.
10.1109/tcc.2026.3743903: The rapid advancement of IoT technology enables edge devices to generate vast amounts of facial data for machine learning. Traditional centralized methods require sensitive data to be uploaded to a semi-trusted cloud, increasing privacy risks. Federated learning addresses this by keeping data local and reducing computational demands, but the uploaded model gradients are vulnerable to attacks that can reconstruct images. Current privacy protection methods struggle to balance communication efficiency with attribute privacy protection, especially for identity-related features. Existing methods often provide insufficient protection against sensitive facial-attribute inference while attempting to preserve the usability of protected data. To address these issues, this work proposes FedDP, a federated learning based reversible face differential privacy protection method. It integrates a pre-trained StyleGAN2 generator and a lightweight latent space encryptor to reversibly encrypt facial identity in the latent space, allowing dynamic data recovery with a key and adjustable privacy strength via the privacy budget. In addition, FedDP reduces the risk of sensitive facial-attribute inference by applying image-specific latent-space encryption and a unified local differential privacy mechanism to the complete encrypted latent representation. FedDP does not identify semantic attributes or assign separate attribute-level privacy budgets during the protection process. Clients apply latent space encryption and local differential privacy noise, while the server adds noise to aggregated updates, ensuring end-to-end protection. Experiments show that FedDP achieves 99% feature reversibility, allows the overall privacy level to be adjusted through the unified privacy budgets, and limits the ResNet-based multi-attribute inference attack success rate to 2.15% when all 10 target attributes are correctly inferred, effectively balancing usability and privacy.
10.1109/tmm.2026.3746073: Data incompleteness and privacy preservation are critical challenges in federated incomplete multi-view clustering. Although recent studies have proposed several solutions, they often suffer from widespread view-missing issues and the difficulty of establishing cross-client consensus under privacy constraints, which hinders reliable missing-data recovery and high-quality representation learning. To address these issues, we propose a structure-guided missing-data recovery framework for federated incomplete multi-view scenarios. Specifically, each client constructs a dynamic anchor graph to capture local structural relationships and performs reliable missing-view data recovery via anchor-based reconstruction. Global structural information is introduced to constrain this recovery process, thereby improving the consistency and reliability of the recovered data. Concurrently, a compact-statistics communication mechanism is designed to exchange pseudo-labels and centroid matrices for global consensus building. The resulting global consensus labels guide representation learning and structural alignment, while consensus centroids enhance semantic consistency across clients. Furthermore, the framework avoids explicit construction of dense affinity matrices and achieves linear complexity with respect to the number of samples via implicit computation, significantly reducing communication overhead and computational cost. Extensive experiments on eight benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior clustering performance over existing federated methods, and outperforms centralized multi-view clustering approaches in terms of both communication and computational efficiency.
10.1109/tcomm.2026.3745158: Federated Learning (FL) has gained widespread adoption for distributed model training due to its ability to preserve privacy and deliver promising learning performance. However, the limited availability of communication resources can significantly slow down the training process. To address this issue, this paper proposes two gradient compression schemes based on Lempel-Ziv (LZ) coding: Lossy Lempel-Ziv with element-wise distortion$p$(LLZ-$p$) and Lossy Lempel-Ziv with Side Information (LLZ-SI). The LLZ-$p$algorithm exploits the inherent redundancy within local gradients and introduces a controlled distortion into the vanilla Lempel-Ziv scheme. Our convergence analysis demonstrates that LLZ-$p$can not only notably reduce communication costs, but also achieve a sublinear convergence rate comparable to that of its lossless counterpart. LLZ-SI further enhances compression by exploiting historical gradient information available at both clients and the server, effectively balancing the compression of current and past gradients. Extensive experiments on various datasets and learning models demonstrate that the proposed LZ-based schemes reduce communication by 58% without degrading accuracy and by up to 90% while maintaining nearly the same learning performance.
10.1109/tce.2026.3745493: Early stroke identification in consumer home environments is challenging due to sudden symptom onset, low public awareness, reliance on observer-dependent screening, overlapping non-stroke manifestations, and the lack of continuous multimodal monitoring. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Edge-Enabled Federated BEFAST, a lightweight multimodal Consumer Internet of Medical Things (CIoMT) framework that operationalizes the clinically used BEFAST triage guideline into measurable behavioral indicators derived from wearable motion sensing, speech analysis, and vision-based facial cues. Each modality is processed locally using compact deeplearning models executed on consumer-grade edge devices, while an interpretable edge-level fusion mechanism generates real-time stroke-consistent screening decisions and records stroke onset time based on the first detected BEFAST-aligned abnormality. To handle issues like data privacy, limited labeled stroke samples, and strong inter-user behavioral heterogeneity across homes, the framework employs a federated transfer learning (FTL) strategy. Local models are adapted to individual users under non-IID data distributions while sharing only model updates for global optimization without exposing raw signals. Experimental evaluation using publicly available multimodal datasets under realistic federated settings demonstrates the feasibility, scalability, and effectiveness of the proposed approach for early stroke symptom screening. The proposed system advances consumer-electronics driven healthcare by enabling timely intervention, objective decision support, and privacy-preserving AI-assisted stroke monitoring in ambient-intelligence homes.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3745458: Large-scale edge IoT systems increasingly rely on multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) to coordinate distributed devices for compute-intensive tasks. However, existing MADRL paradigms often require a centralized critic or cross device information sharing, which can expose devices' local states and thus raise privacy concerns. This paper develops fedV, a privacy-aware federated deep reinforcement learning framework for volunteer-supported edge computing, where opportunistic volunteer devices are selected to elastically extend edge capacity. Due to intermittent and untrusted volunteer resources, MADRL-based coordination becomes a highly challenging long term optimization problem. To preserve multi-agent cooperation without raw-state exposure, fedV adopts a hierarchical learning architecture based on two-tier federated learning. Specifically, IoT-side agents are trained from local observations, while an edge-side agent aggregates privacy-preserving representations to make global decisions under strict device-side privacy protection. We further introduce a reversed-reward weighted aggregation rule to improve learning efficiency under heterogeneous and non-IID multi-agent interactions. Compared with representative baselines, fedV improves the long-term average reward by up to 30.9% and the converged reward by up to 54.6%. These simulations demonstrate that fedV achieves robust schedulability and scalability under different edge-capacity settings.
10.1109/tccn.2026.3745650: Data-driven decision-making is a key enabler of intelligent enterprises, yet centralized machine learning (ML) poses privacy and efficiency risks. Federated learning (FL) offers a decentralized solution. Still, it faces 1) high communication cost, 2) vulnerability to poisoning and inference attacks, and 3) degraded performance on non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. This paper presentsFedAnil+++, a privacy-preserving and communication-efficient FL model with three phases: (i) dynamic gradient compression, (ii) multi-layer protection via cosine similarity (CS) filtering, CKKS-FHE, and blockchain aggregation, and (iii) personalized FL (PFL) through clustering and adversarial learning. Experiments on FEMNIST, CIFAR-10, and TON-IoT show thatFedAnil+++boosts accuracy by 15.75%, cuts communication by 25.87%, and reduces computation by 4.5% over baselines. Privacy metrics, Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, Shannon entropy, and correlation analysis confirm that CKKS-FHE effectively conceals sensitive patterns. The implementation ofFedAnil+++is publicly available on GitHubhttps://github.com/rezafotohi/FedAnilPlusPlusPlus
10.1109/tnse.2026.3746198: Federated unlearning has become a necessary mechanism for removing poisoned, sensitive, or withdrawn data from federated models. However, existing unlearning protocols often treat a client's acknowledgment of deletion as evidence of compliance. This assumption leaves a critical false unlearning vulnerability: malicious clients can return updates that appear consistent with unlearning while retaining backdoor knowledge, which may subsequently contaminate the global model through aggregation. The central problem is therefore to distinguish genuine forgetting from deceptive compliance during the unlearning process and to prevent untrustworthy clients from participating in later training rounds. To address this problem, this paper proposes a multidimensional dynamic trust evaluation framework that transforms unlearning verification into privacy-preserving, evidence-driven trust inference.To prevent attackers from identifying and overfitting the trap probes, the probe reference gradient is protected by CKKS approximate homomorphic encryption, while Johnson-Lindenstrauss random projection compressing. The resulting behavioral and quality trust values are fused through entropy-based weighting and evolved across rounds using Markov trust updating.Experimental results under false unlearning attack demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively identifies malicious clients, suppresses residual backdoor effects, and provides a more robust trust-evaluation solution for securing federated unlearning.
10.1109/tce.2026.3746042: Statistical heterogeneity and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data remain major challenges in federated learning, particularly for agricultural terrain mapping where geographically distributed sensing devices collect highly diverse remote sensing data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an Adaptive Local Aggregation (ALA)-based personalized federated learning framework that improves client-specific model initialization while preserving the standard federated learning communication and global aggregation protocol. Rather than directly replacing local models with the received global model, the proposed framework adaptively initializes selected higher-layer parameters using learnable client-specific aggregation weights, thereby balancing globally shared knowledge with local personalization prior to client-side training. The proposed framework is evaluated on four agricultural remote sensing datasets, namely AgriFieldNet, BigEarthNetv1, BigEarthNetv2, and CropHarvest, together with three benchmark image classification datasets, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, under heterogeneous federated learning settings. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements in global classification accuracy and convergence behaviour compared with state-of-the-art federated learning methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed framework for privacy-preserving agricultural terrain mapping under heterogeneous client data distributions.
10.1109/tcss.2026.3738284: Federated learning (FL) breaks down data silos through distributed collaboration. Due to the limited motivation of participants, incentive mechanisms are essential for encouraging sustained participation.
